title: The Last Man Who Knew Everything — from Geisa to Rome, and Down into the Burning World
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: The Buchonian Boy (Geisa, Fulda, and the Rhön Hills)

stops.name: Geisa on the Ulster — the birth of the polymath
stops.campa: On the second of May, feast of his name-saint Athanasius, the ninth and last child is born to Johann Kircher, doctor of theology and bailiff of Haselstein, in the little town of Geisa below the Rhön. He is so late a child that even he will never be certain of his year. He takes from this soil the names Bucho and Fuldensis, and grows up grave and devouring, a boy who reads everything. His father sets private tutors over him and hires the town rabbi to teach him Hebrew. The mountains of the Buchonia ring him, and beneath them, unknown, run the fires he will one day map.
suggested_refs: portrait of Athanasius Kircher from Mundus Subterraneus (1664)

stops.name: Fulda — the Jesuit college and the abbey of Boniface
stops.campa: From 1614 the boy attends the Jesuit Gymnasium at Fulda, city of Saint Boniface's tomb, capital of the prince-abbots his father served. Here he masters Latin and Greek and secretly, at night, the Hebrew and the mathematics his masters do not teach in daylight. He is quick past his years and hides it, having learned that too much brilliance draws the rod. The war-clouds are already gathering over the Empire; the boy studies as though the whole of learning might soon be needed and soon be lost.
suggested_refs: Fulda Cathedral and tomb of St Boniface

stops.name: Fulda stadium — trampled under the Pentecost horses and rising unharmed
stops.campa: At the Pentecost cavalry-race the schoolboy is jostled and flung from his place down into the stadium, directly into the path of the charging horses. He presses his face to the earth and curls his body as tight as it will go while the whole race thunders over him. The dust settles; the crowd expects a corpse. He rises entirely unharmed and uninjured. It is the first of the deliverances he will count all his life — the sign, he believes, that Providence keeps him for some great work not yet begun.
stops.quote: I pressed my face to the ground and curled my body as tightly as I could, and the horses rushed over me, yet I arose entirely unharmed and uninjured.

segments.name: The Novice in the War (Paderborn, the Ice, the Gallows)

stops.name: Paderborn — the novitiate and the miraculous cure
stops.campa: In October he enters the novitiate of the Society of Jesus at Paderborn. He arrives already stricken: skating on the ice he has torn himself with a hidden hernia, and his legs, frozen and gangrenous, are declared incurable by the surgeon. Kircher tells no one but the Virgin. One night before her miracle-working image he prays; he wakes, and both ailments have wholly vanished — the hernia gone, the legs whole. The examining surgeon is confounded. The same month the Bohemian revolt breaks out at Prague; the Thirty Years' War has begun, and the boy is inside it.
stops.quote: Both ailments had been completely cured; the hernia had also entirely vanished.

stops.name: The frozen Rhine near Düsseldorf — carried away on the ice-floe
stops.campa: In January, as the fiercely anti-Jesuit army advances, Kircher and two companions flee Paderborn through deep snow, penniless and begging bread. They come to the Rhine, frozen over, and start across. Midstream the ice cracks; the floe on which Kircher stands breaks free and bears him away downstream, a man marooned on a drifting island of ice. He leaps from fragment to fragment, then throws himself into the black water and swims, and comes ashore near Neuss entirely unharmed and uninjured. Twice now the river and the frost have refused him.
stops.quote: Carried downstream by the rushing waters, stranded on what was effectively an ice island, I made my way and came ashore entirely unharmed.

stops.name: Cologne — refuge and the study of philosophy
stops.campa: He reaches Catholic Cologne and its great university, and there resumes his study of philosophy, science, and the classical tongues. In the shadow of the unfinished cathedral he steadies himself after the ice; the war has made a wanderer of a novice, but it has also shown him that he is preserved. He reads voraciously — mathematics, languages, the sciences of light and sound and the loadstone — laying the foundations of the universal knowledge for which he will one day be called Germanus incredibilis, the incredible German.

stops.name: Koblenz — the young teacher at the confluence
stops.campa: For his regency he is sent to teach at the Jesuit school in Koblenz, where the Moselle pours into the Rhine at the Deutsches Eck. Here he first shows the double gift that will define him — the languages of Scripture and the machinery of the world. He teaches grammar and mathematics, and privately turns already to the greater riddles: the loadstone that turns north, the sun that draws the flower, the tongues of the ancient East. He is still crossing hostile ground; the war does not yet let him rest.

stops.name: The Valley of Hell — stripped for the gallows, spared for his calm
stops.campa: Crossing the war-lines through a defile his account calls the Valley of Hell, Kircher falls among heretical horsemen. They strip him, beat him, and make ready to hang him from a tree. He does not struggle; he prays, and stands so calm before his death that one soldier is struck to the heart and cries out that his hands will stay innocent of this man's blood. The rope is put away. They release him, and the very man who spared him gives him provisions for the road. He counts it his fourth deliverance.
stops.quote: I declare that my hands will remain innocent of this man's blood.
stops.quote_source: Kircher, Vita (autobiography) — words of the soldier who spared him

stops.name: Heiligenstadt — mathematics, Hebrew, and the first wonders
stops.campa: At Heiligenstadt in Eichsfeld he teaches mathematics, Hebrew, and Syriac, and begins to stage the marvels that will make his fame — fireworks and moving figures, illusions of light, mechanical curiosities that so astonish the local worthies that some mutter of sorcery. To answer them he must show his art is nature understood, not magic. The reputation runs ahead of him: here is a Jesuit who can make statues speak and shadows move, who reads the dead languages and questions the loadstone. Rome will hear of him.

segments.name: The Egyptian Obsession is Born (Mainz, Speyer, Würzburg)

stops.name: Mainz — ordination to the priesthood
stops.campa: At Mainz, seat of the arch-chancellor of the Empire, Kircher is ordained priest. In these years of theology he also watches the sky through the college telescope and records the spots upon the sun, that same sun whose secret sympathy he believes draws the sunflower round after it. The priest is made; now the scholar's true vocation waits only for a book. He is sent onward for his final probation, his tertianship, to Speyer — and there, on a library errand, his whole life will turn.

stops.name: Speyer — the hieroglyph book that seizes him for life
stops.campa: In his year of spiritual retreat at Speyer he is sent to find a book in the library, and stumbles instead upon a volume figuring the hieroglyphs of an Egyptian obelisk — the reproductions of the Sistine obelisk in Herwart von Hohenburg's Thesaurus. He stares at the beautiful indecipherable signs and is captured utterly. These pictures, he becomes certain, hide the sacred wisdom of the Egyptians, the theology before all theologies. From this hour to his death fifty years on, Egypt will be the burning centre of his mind. He resolves to read what no man since the pharaohs has read.

stops.name: Würzburg — professor, prophetic vision, and flight
stops.campa: From 1629 Kircher holds the chair of mathematics, ethics, and Oriental languages at the Jesuit college of Würzburg, and there publishes his first book, Ars Magnesia, on the loadstone. But in the night, he tells, he is granted a vision of armed men in the courtyard and the town in flames. He warns his brethren; they doubt him. Then the Protestant army of Gustavus Adolphus descends, and in 1631 Würzburg falls. Kircher flees westward with his brilliant pupil Caspar Schott, abandoning his books and papers to the war, carrying only his purpose.

segments.name: Exile Toward the Sun (Lyon, Avignon, the Voyage to Rome)

stops.name: Lyon — the exile reaches France
stops.campa: The fugitive scholar and his pupil struggle across the war-torn Empire — Mainz, Koblenz, and out at last to Lyon in France. Behind him lie the frozen rivers and the gallows-tree and the burning towns of Germany; ahead lies the papal south. He is bound for the light. He carries in his baggage the loadstone and the hieroglyph, and in his head the vast unwritten library of his coming books. The Society directs him to the papal enclave of Avignon, to teach.

stops.name: Avignon — the sunflower clock and the mill-wheel
stops.campa: On papal territory at Avignon Kircher lectures in mathematics and Oriental tongues, and builds in the Jesuit tower his marvels: a chamber of mirrors, an astronomical apparatus, and the wonder that carries his fame across Europe — the sunflower clock, a heliotrope floating on cork in water, its pointer following the sun by what he calls the flower's magnetism, telling the hours. Here too the water-wheel he is studying throws him and tumbles him in its turning; he prays to the Virgin, the wheel stops, and he escapes unharmed. The great Peiresc hears of his sunflower and his Coptic and burns to meet him.
stops.quote: The wheel stopped. I was soon immersed in the water, yet I managed to escape safely and unharmed.

stops.name: Aix-en-Provence — Peiresc, the Coptic, and the lost manuscript
stops.campa: The prince of antiquaries, Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc, draws Kircher to his cabinet at Aix and lays before him Arabic and Coptic manuscripts — among them the mysterious book he ascribes to Barachias Nephi, believed to hold the key to the hieroglyphs. Kircher pores over the Coptic, convinced it is the last living daughter of the pharaohs' tongue and the ladder by which he will climb into Egypt. Peiresc, marvelling and then doubting, comes to suspect the sunflower clock is only a hidden magnet — but he it is who intervenes to send Kircher not to Vienna but to Rome.

stops.name: The sea off the Italian coast — blown to Rome by Providence
stops.campa: The Emperor summons Kircher to Vienna to succeed the dead Kepler as court mathematician. Peiresc pleads that so rare a man belongs in Rome, and the order is rescinded — but too late: Kircher has already embarked for Vienna. His ship is blown off its course, driven down the coast, and lands him in Italy; he reaches Rome before word of the changed destination ever finds him. He counts it Providence: the very winds have carried him to the city of the obelisks. The last of his sea-deliverances sets him down at the centre of the world.

segments.name: The Descent into the Burning World (the South, Sicily, Vesuvius)

stops.name: Rome, Collegio Romano — the chair and the first Coptic grammar
stops.campa: Kircher takes up the chair of mathematics, physics, and Oriental languages at the Collegio Romano — the post he will hold, in one form or another, for the rest of his life. In 1636 he publishes the Prodromus Coptus, the first grammar of the Coptic tongue printed in Europe, and announces to the learned world that the door to Egypt stands open. From this cell in the heart of Rome he will send out forty years of books on every science under heaven. The wanderer has arrived; now the whole earth will come to him.

stops.name: Malta — confessor to the convert prince
stops.campa: On the last day of May, Kircher lands in Malta as confessor to Landgrave Friedrich of Hesse-Darmstadt, the great German prince lately turned from Lutheranism to the Roman faith. Among the knights of Saint John he teaches mathematics at the Jesuit college and studies the island's antiquities and its strange fossil-teeth, the glossopetrae he takes for petrified serpents' tongues. But the ground itself calls to him: across the water Etna smokes and Stromboli burns, and Kircher resolves to learn whether all the fires of the earth are one fire, joined beneath the sea.

stops.name: The Strait of Messina — the subterranean roar
stops.campa: Returning north through Sicily, Kircher stands at the Strait of Messina and hears, beneath the whirlpools of Charybdis, a subterranean rumbling and din — the sound, he becomes sure, of the earth's inner waters and fires labouring in their channels. Here the whole vision of the Mundus Subterraneus is conceived: a globe not solid but everywhere gaping, threaded with fire-veins and water-veins, its volcanoes the breath-pipes of a single burning heart. He crosses to the mainland to see the fire for himself, and walks straight into the wrath of the earth.

stops.name: Calabria — cast down by the great earthquake
stops.campa: In Calabria the ground itself rises against him. A subterranean racket like chariots driven at top speed throws Kircher flat on his face upon the earth; the great earthquake of 1638 kills some ten thousand souls. Walking on through the ruin, his party comes upon nothing but the cadavers of cities and the horrific ruins of castles. Where other men would flee, Kircher reads: this is the living proof of his hidden world, the fire beneath breaking the crust above. He turns his face toward the smoking cone of Vesuvius, determined to look into the mouth of it.
stops.quote: A subterranean racket and din, similar to chariots driven at top speed, laid me low, suddenly dashed down with my face flat on the ground; and we came upon nothing but cadavers of cities and horrific ruins of castles.

stops.name: Vesuvius — lowered by rope into the smoking crater
stops.campa: By night Kircher climbs the four thousand feet to the summit of Vesuvius, the mountain on the very brink of eruption. At the lip he hears horrible bellowings and roarings and chokes on an unexpressible stink from the vents. Then, with his pantometer, he has himself lowered on a rope down into the crater itself, into the belly of the fire, to measure its dimensions and gaze upon the pool boiling with an everlasting gushing forth and streaming of smoke and flames. He looks, he later writes, into the very kitchen of Nature, the workshop of Pluto — and comes up alive to describe it to the world.
stops.quote: I saw what I could not have imagined... boiling with an everlasting gushing forth and streaming of smoke and flames, and all up and down everywhere cragged and broken.

segments.name: The Universal Books (Rome, the Obelisks, the Music of the World)

stops.name: Rome — Magnes, the loadstone and the harmony of the world
stops.campa: In 1641 Kircher publishes Magnes, sive de Arte Magnetica, his great book of the loadstone. For him magnetism is no mere trick of iron but the very principle that binds the cosmos: the sun draws the planets and the sunflower as the loadstone draws the needle, God draws the soul, love draws all things to their like. The whole world is a web of hidden sympathies and attractions, one vast magnet. In his museum he builds magnetic oracles and self-moving figures to display the secret force, and teaches that to know the magnet is to glimpse the architecture of creation.
stops.quote: Nature everywhere is magnetic; the whole world is bound together by hidden chains of attraction.
stops.quote_source: paraphrase of Kircher, Magnes sive de Arte Magnetica (1641)

stops.name: Rome — Musurgia Universalis and the cat-piano
stops.campa: In the great Musurgia Universalis Kircher sets out the music of the whole world — the harmony of the spheres, the songs of birds transcribed on the stave, the noise-making organs of bees, the water-driven automatic organs that play without hands. Here he records the Katzenklavier, the cat-piano, contrived to lift a melancholy prince: cats chosen by the pitch of their voices, ranged in boxes, their tails pricked by hammers under the keys so that pressing them makes each cry its note in tune. The universe itself, he teaches, is God's instrument, and all its creatures voices in one immense concord.
stops.quote: The cats, arranged according to the pitch of their voices, would furnish a music as their tails were pricked, and the prince's melancholy was dispelled.
stops.quote_source: after Kircher, Musurgia Universalis (1650), Book VI

stops.name: Piazza Navona — the obelisk raised, the hieroglyphs 'read'
stops.campa: Pope Innocent X gives Kircher the shattered Egyptian obelisk before the Palazzo Pamphilj and bids him restore and read it while Bernini raises it over the Fountain of the Four Rivers. Where the stone is broken away, Kircher supplies from his own mind the hieroglyphs he is certain once stood there — and when the lost fragments are recovered, he declares they match his prediction exactly. On the twelfth of June the fountain is unveiled, the obelisk soaring on its rock, the Pamphilj dove at its peak, and his Latin readings cut into the plaques below: a mystic hymn to Osiris, gloriously and wholly wrong, standing to this day.

stops.name: Rome — Oedipus Aegyptiacus, the whole of Egypt deciphered
stops.campa: Between 1652 and 1655 Kircher publishes the four vast folios of Oedipus Aegyptiacus, the crown of his Egyptian labour — a comparative theology of all the ancient nations, in which he claims to have solved the riddle of the hieroglyphs as the Sphinx's riddle was solved by Oedipus. Every sign, he holds, is a whole allegory of divine mysteries: a single carved bird unfolds under his pen into paragraphs of Neoplatonic wisdom. It is the most learned wrong book ever written; not one glyph is truly read, yet within it Egyptology itself is born, and Europe first beholds the sacred writing whole.

stops.name: Piazza della Minerva — the elephant and the obelisk
stops.campa: For Pope Alexander VII, Kircher interprets a small Egyptian obelisk unearthed by the Dominicans, and helps devise its emblem: Bernini sets the ancient stone upon the back of a marble elephant before Santa Maria sopra Minerva, so that the beast bears wisdom's monument on its strength. Kircher supplies again the reading of its glyphs, a further sermon in stone on divine light and Egyptian priesthood. The little elephant, called by the Romans il pulcino della Minerva, still carries its obelisk, one more of the pharaohs' stones re-raised by the Jesuit who believed he could read them.
suggested_refs: Bernini's Elephant and Obelisk, Piazza della Minerva

segments.name: The Whole Earth in One Mind (the Subterranean World, Ark, Babel, China, Death)

stops.name: Mentorella — the shrine restored and the pilgrim's heart
stops.campa: In the mountains east of Rome, at Guadagnolo, Kircher rediscovers the ruined church where, tradition holds, the hunter Eustace saw the Cross between a stag's antlers. He raises the funds and restores the Sanctuary of the Mentorella, and makes it his soul's own place, retreating there year on year. To this high lonely shrine, when he dies, his heart will be carried and buried, though his body lies in the Gesù at Rome. The man who mapped the whole burning earth keeps for himself this small holy mountain, and asks that his heart rest where the Cross once shone above the stag.

stops.name: Rome — Mundus Subterraneus, the hollow burning earth
stops.campa: Out of Vesuvius and the earthquake comes the Mundus Subterraneus, the first great book of the underground world. Kircher declares that the whole earth is not solid but everywhere gaping and hollowed with empty rooms and spaces, threaded with channels of fire and veins of water joining every volcano to every other and to a central hearth of flame within. The tides are the breathing of a subterranean ocean; the mountains are the vent-holes, or breath-pipes, of Nature. Two centuries before Symmes cries his hollow earth, Kircher has already lit the fire at its core and drawn the map of Pluto's kingdom.
stops.quote: The whole Earth is not solid but everywhere gaping, and hollowed with empty rooms and spaces, and hidden burrows and fire-vaults.

stops.name: Rome — China Illustrata and the Nestorian stone
stops.campa: Never having left Italy, Kircher assembles from the letters of his brethren in the East the China Illustrata, and lays the whole Ming empire before Europe — its cities and rivers and gods, its dragons studied as gravely as its mountains. Chief of its treasures is the Nestorian stele of Xi'an, whose Chinese and Syriac he prints and renders into Latin, proving to his own joy that the Cross reached China a thousand years before: Christianity was there before the missionaries. Many across Europe cry forgery; Kircher holds firm. From his cell the unmoving Jesuit has annexed the farthest East to the map of the one true faith.
suggested_refs: Kircher's map of China and its dragons

stops.name: Rome — Arca Noë, the Ark rebuilt to scale
stops.campa: In the Arca Noë Kircher reconstructs Noah's Ark exactly as Scripture built it, and reckons with a quartermaster's rigour how every kind of beast was stowed, fed, and watered through the Flood — the decks apportioned, the fodder measured, the serpents and the great cats each in their place. The Deluge is true and total, and the Ark its floating cosmos; he draws it plank by plank. Where others read the Flood as a parable, Kircher engineers it, and shows the world the very vessel in which all living kinds rode out the drowning of the earth.

stops.name: The Museum Kircherianum — the speaking statue and the cabinet of wonders
stops.campa: In the Collegio Romano Kircher gathers the age's most famous Wunderkammer, the Museum Kircherianum: obelisks and fossils and Egyptian gods, magic lanterns that throw demons on the wall, magnetic oracles, perpetual-motion toys, and the speaking statue — a figure joined by hidden spiral tubes to the street outside, so that it answers passers-by and startles the whole college with a voice from nowhere. Cardinals and princes and travellers from every land come to marvel. The wandering novice who once hid his cleverness now presides over a whole theatre of the world's wonders, the last man, they say, who knew everything.

stops.name: Rome — Turris Babel, the Tower and the scattering of tongues
stops.campa: In the Turris Babel Kircher raises Nimrod's tower to scale and proves by geometry that it could never have reached the Moon: to lift so vast a mass to heaven would have unbalanced the whole earth and tumbled it from its place. From the tower's fall he traces the confusion of tongues, mapping how the one Adamic language broke into all the languages of the world, and drawing the descent of every nation from the sons of Noah. It is his last great book of sacred history — the Ark, the Tower, and the peopling of the earth, the whole story of mankind engineered and diagrammed by the incredible German.
suggested_refs: table of the descent of languages

stops.name: Rome — the death of the last man who knew everything
stops.campa: On the twenty-seventh of November, in his cell in Rome after nearly fifty years, Athanasius Kircher dies, close to eighty years old. He has read the hieroglyphs and been wrong; mapped the fire in the earth and been right before his time; built the cat-piano and the speaking statue; rebuilt the Ark and the Tower; annexed China and Egypt to the faith; and survived the ice, the gallows, the mill-wheel, the earthquake, and the crater. His body is laid in the church of the Gesù; his heart is borne up to the Mentorella. The last man who knew everything is gathered to the burning world he loved.
